summary: For 7-8 year olds learning time-unit and calendar facts: 60 seconds in a minute, the names and irregular lengths of the twelve months, and that a leap year has 366 days and usually comes every four years. Factual recall of seconds/minutes and month names is usually a strength; the conceptual depth lies in (1) the uneven 31/30/28 month-length pattern (February has 29 days in a leap year), (2) the non-decimal grouping of 60 for seconds and minutes, and (3) WHY leap years exist - the Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun, so the leftover quarter-days add up to about one extra day every four years. (Because the true leftover is slightly less than a quarter, a few century years such as 1900 and 2100 are not leap years; this detail is beyond the core objective.) Research reports most children do not connect time units to the Earth's motion at all.
misconceptions: Assumes all months are the same length (e.g. 30 days each)
Treats the leap-year rule as arbitrary, unconnected to the Earth's orbit
Over-applies base-10 to seconds and minutes (90 seconds = 0.9 of a minute; 1 minute 30 seconds = 130 seconds)

activities.title: Advance a four-year calendar cycle and watch February change
steps: Step through four years one at a time on a calendar dial or a strip showing four Februaries in a row.
On years one, two and three, note that February has 28 days; on the fourth year watch a 29th day appear and the year-counter go from 365 to 366.
Say aloud what changes and what stays the same across the four years, then predict which upcoming calendar year will be the next leap year.
Tap or reveal each month in turn to pop up its length, and sort or describe the uneven 31/30/28 pattern as a shape, not just a list.
activities.insight: 'Every four years' is not an arbitrary rule to memorise - the extra day actually appears only on the fourth turn, and February is the month that gains it, while month lengths follow a lumpy repeating pattern.

activities.title: Build the leap day from the Earth's orbit
steps: Using an orbit model, card tokens, or a tally, give each year its length as 'about 365 and a quarter days' and set aside the leftover quarter each year.
After four years, snap the four leftover quarter-days together into one whole extra day.
Explain in your own words where the extra day came from and why we only add it roughly every four years, then name the day we add it to (29 February).
activities.insight: The leap day exists because the Earth's orbit takes about 365 and a quarter days; the leftover quarter-day each year builds up to one whole day about every four years, which we add to February.

activities.title: Group seconds into minutes at exactly 60
steps: Count seconds on a stopwatch or a number line marked in seconds, and mark where a full group of 60 closes into one minute.
Work out how many seconds are in one and a half minutes, saying why it is 90 (60 + 30) and not 150 - rather than applying base-10 place value (treating 1.5 minutes as 1.5 x 100 = 150 seconds).
Convert a two-way example such as '1 minute 30 seconds = [ ] seconds' and '90 seconds = [ ] minute [ ] seconds', regrouping at 60 each time.
activities.insight: Seconds and minutes group in 60s, not 100s, so conversions require regrouping at 60 rather than applying base-10 place value.

activities.title: Recall and sort the facts
steps: Name the months in order and state how many days each has.
Sort the months into 31-day, 30-day, and 'other' (February) groups.
Answer fact questions: '1 minute = [ ] seconds', 'how often is a leap year?', 'how many days in a leap year?'
Use a mnemonic such as knuckles or '30 days hath September' to recall which months are shorter.
activities.insight: The core recall facts - 60 seconds, month names and lengths, and that a leap year has 366 days and usually comes every four years - need to be fluent so attention can go to the harder conceptual links.

checkQuestion: Ask the fact, then the reason. (A) 'A leap year has 366 days instead of 365 — one extra day. Where does that extra day come from, and why do we only add it every four years?' (B) 'How many seconds is one and a half minutes, and how do you know?' Also, in passing: 'Which months have fewer than 31 days?'
checkAnswer: (A) The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go once round the Sun; the leftover quarter-days build up to one whole day roughly every four years, which we add to February. (B) 90 seconds, because 60 seconds make one minute, so one and a half minutes = 60 + 30. Names the shorter months (Feb; the 30-day months).
